title: Covert Technical Collection Platforms: Physical Implant and Device Intrusion Operations
body:
The physical layer of intelligence collection in GLMZ operates in a domain that digital surveillance cannot reach: the interior of hardware itself. Covert technical collection operations targeting corporate facilities rely on the physical introduction of modified components, secondary devices, and parasitic sensor systems into target infrastructure. The practice, known among practitioners as 'seeding,' has become a primary methodology for penetrating corporate networks that maintain genuine air gaps between internal systems and external connectivity—a category that includes weapons R&D divisions, pharmaceutical formula repositories, and financial arbitrage algorithm vaults, all of which learned the cost of network connectivity after the breach events of the 2060s.

The most common seeding vector is the corporate supply chain. Hardware components—cooling fans, power regulators, network switches, even replacement neural interface charging cradles—pass through multiple manufacturing and distribution intermediaries before reaching their final installation point, and each handoff represents an opportunity for component modification or substitution. Intelligence operations targeting GLMZ's corporate tier have successfully introduced modified components at the point of third-party refurbishment, during warehouse transit through the Calumet Logistics Corridor, and at the installation stage through compromised facilities contractors. The modified components function normally in all testable parameters while hosting secondary firmware or physical sensor arrays that exfiltrate data through channels invisible to standard security audits—most commonly through manipulation of electromagnetic emissions, power line signaling, or acoustic side channels.

Human-carried intrusion represents a higher-risk but faster-yield alternative. Operatives or unwitting couriers introduce physical collection devices into target facilities under cover of routine access—maintenance visits, catering service, equipment delivery, or the escort of external consultants. The devices themselves have shrunk dramatically with advances in fabrication technology: current-generation audio and electromagnetic collection nodes can be embedded in objects as small as a standard wall anchor or power outlet faceplate, and are designed to be visually indistinguishable from legitimate infrastructure components. Detection requires either active RF sweep protocols—which most corporate facilities conduct only during elevated alert states—or the kind of meticulous physical inventory that large facilities cannot practically maintain.

Counter-seeding operations have become a significant line item in corporate security budgets. The most rigorous implementations involve hardware verification chains using cryptographic component authentication, physical inspection of all inbound equipment using X-ray and acoustic imaging arrays at receiving docks, and randomized replacement cycles for installed hardware that limit the operational window of any implanted device. The Northwall Security Consortium—a shared-services arrangement among seven Lakeshore Tower corporate tenants—operates what is considered the most sophisticated counter-seeding program in GLMZ, employing twelve full-time hardware forensics specialists. Despite this, a publicly reported incident in 2179 revealed that a modified HVAC controller had operated undetected in a Consortium member's server room for fourteen months, collecting thermal side-channel data from compute operations below.
headings: The Physical Layer Beyond Digital Surveillance
